idiom_name: abstract Implementor with pure virtuals held by std::unique_ptr
implementation_notes: In C++ the two hierarchies are hand-written: an Implementor abstract class with pure virtual primitives and an Abstraction base holding it by std::unique_ptr (raw pointer before C++11), with each refined abstraction forwarding to the primitives; the language contributes library pieces rather than the structure. The degenerate single-implementor case has its own idiomatic form, the pimpl (compilation firewall) idiom, which cppreference and Sutter both document as removing compile-time dependencies and stabilising the ABI - it is not a two-hierarchy Bridge, so choose it for hiding and rebuild cascades rather than for independent extensibility. Keep the classic virtual Bridge when both sides genuinely grow, and prefer closed-set value dispatch (std::variant plus std::visit) when you own every implementor and want no vtable and no allocation.
pitfalls: The implementor is held by pointer: give the abstraction a virtual destructor and decide copy semantics explicitly, since the generated copy duplicates the pointer (two owners, one implementor).

Every forwarded call is an indirect call through the vtable and cannot be inlined across translation units without link-time optimisation (cppreference makes the same point for pimpl); keep the forwarding functions thin.
A template implementation class cannot be hidden behind the seam the way a non-template one can - erase the template from the interface or the compile-time dependency returns.

variants.name: pimpl (compilation firewall) with one hidden implementor
variants.idiom_name: std::unique_ptr<impl> over a forward-declared nested class
variants.implementation_notes: The visible class declares struct impl; (or class impl;) and holds std::unique_ptr<impl>, with impl defined in the .cpp file, so private data changes never recompile clients and the ABI stays stable - the GoF book calls this the one-implementor degenerate case of Bridge, and cppreference documents it as the compilation-firewall technique. Use it for hiding and rebuild cascades, not for independent extensibility: there is no implementor hierarchy and no second axis.
pitfalls: std::unique_ptr with an incomplete type requires the destructor and move operations to be user-declared and defined out of line in the .cpp file; defaulting them in the header is a hard error.
pimpl hides private data but not the public interface and provides no abstraction hierarchy, so it does not give two-axis extensibility.
Each object allocates its implementation separately: numerous small short-lived objects pay an allocation per instance, which is what the fast-pimpl/opaque-buffer trick tries to avoid.

variants.name: Closed-set value dispatch with std::variant and std::visit
variants.idiom_name: std::variant<Implementors...> + std::visit over an overload set
variants.implementation_notes: Model the implementor set as a std::variant of concrete renderers and dispatch with std::visit (or the member visit overload), so the abstraction holds a value instead of a pointer: no inheritance, no vtable, no allocation, and the call can be inlined. The price is closure - the implementor set is fixed in the type, so adding one is a recompile of every visitor - which makes this the right choice when you own all implementors and the alternative would be an exhaustive-selection switch.
pitfalls: The implementor set is closed in the variant's type: a new implementor changes the type and every visit must be recompiled and updated (that is the safety you are buying).
All alternatives must be complete types here, so implementors cannot be hidden behind a translation-unit boundary the way a pimpl can.
Visitor overload sets built by inheriting lambdas accept implicit conversions, so a broad overload can silently capture the wrong alternative - keep each overload's parameter type exact.
